body: There is variation in the features of individuals of the same species.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Variation can be caused by information in the genome and by the environment, but only variation caused by information in the genome is heritable (can be passed on to offspring).

body: Due to variation, some individuals within a species have features that make them better adapted to complete and survive in their environment.

body: Better adapted individuals are more likely to reproduce and pass heritable adaptations (caused by genetic variation) on to the next generation.

body: This ‘natural selection’ of better adapted individuals causes advantageous features to become more common in each generation of offspring.

body: Natural selection can cause the common features of a species to change (evolve) over generations.

title: Gamma rays are always higher energy (or power), or more dangerous, than other frequencies of EM radiation.
body: EM waves transfer their energy in 'chunks' or 'packets'. The energy transferred by one 'packet' of radiation (and so its ionising ability) does depend on frequency. But the power of a beam of radiation depends on the intensity of the radiation too.

title: The majority of pupils struggle to differentiate between ionising and non–ionising radiation.
body: Explicitly teach that non–ionising radiation is not able to force electrons off atoms – it cannot turn atoms into ions. What it may be able to do is cause heating by increasing the movement of particles and therefore temperature of the substance.

body: Refraction is when waves travel from one transparent medium to another, causing a change in direction.

body: When waves slow down, they turn towards the normal line (angle of incidence > angle of refraction).

body: When waves speed up, they turn away from the normal line (angle of incidence < angle of refraction).

body: Refraction can be investigated using a clear rectangular block, ray box and narrow slit, pencil, paper and a protractor.

body: At a boundary to a medium where the wave speed increases, waves are refracted away from the normal.

body: If the angle of incidence is too big (bigger than the critical angle) the waves will undergo total internal reflection.

body: The critical angle is the greatest angle of incidence before total internal reflection occurs.

title: critical angle
body: The critical angle is the greatest angle of incidence before total internal reflection occurs for a boundary to a medium with greater wave speed.

body: A triangular prism can produce a colour spectrum from white light, showing it is a mixture of all visible wavelengths.

body: From red to violet in the spectrum, frequency increases and wavelength decreases. Higher frequencies refract further.

body: Opaque objects transmit no incident light. Their colour depends on which wavelengths of incident light are reflected.

title: Pupils assume that the colours of light will mix in the same way that paints mix.
body: Make it explicit in your teaching that the primary colours of light (red, green and blue) are different, and mix differently, to the primary colours of paint that pupils may have been taught elsewhere (e.g. red, yellow and blue).

body: Converging lenses can produce an inverted image on a screen by refracting light.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Rays parallel to the principal axis are refracted to the principal focus of a converging lens (at the focal length).
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: The image distance and size (magnification) depend on the power of the lens and the object distance.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: As the object distance decreases, the image distance and size both increase, until the object reaches the focal length.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: If the object is too close to the lens, the rays leaving the lens are parallel/diverging, images can't form on a screen.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: diminished
body: Diminished means smaller than an object’s real size. It is the opposite of magnified.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: converging
body: Light rays are converging if they are coming together to a point where they will meet.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: principal focus
body: The principal focus is the point to which parallel rays (from distant objects) are focused.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: focal length
body: The focal length is the distance between the centre of a lens and the principal focus.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: lens power
body: The greater the power of a lens, the greater the angles through which light is refracted and the shorter the focal length.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils often think there is only one ray of light for each point of light on the image.
body: Many rays of light pass through the lens from each point on the object, but all the rays from a single point arrive at a single point at the image distance. The rays from each point on the object arrive at corresponding points at the same distance.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In cameras and the human eye, the required image distance < the object distance. The image is diminished and inverted.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In projectors, the required image distance > the object distance. The image is magnified and inverted.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A ray incident on a converging lens parallel to the principal axis is refracted to pass through principal focus.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A ray incident on the centre of a converging lens is not refracted.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: A ray incident on a converging lens from the principal focus is refracted so it becomes parallel to the principal axis.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: object distance

title: image distance

attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: focal length

attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: principal axis
body: The principal axis is a line through the centre of a lens, 90° to the optical axis of the lens.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Covering over half of a lens will block out rays of light from half the object and the image will appear cut in half.
body: Talk about many rays of light passing through the lens from each point of the object and show pupils that blocking half the lens keeps the same image, only less bright.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: When rays of light are brought to a focus a real image forms. A real image can be projected onto a screen.

body: Virtual images occur at points where rays appear to (but do not actually) originate from. They cannot form on a screen.

body: The size and position of a virtual image is found by drawing virtual rays to find where rays appear to originate from.

body: Upright virtual images are produced by diverging lenses, and objects within a focal length of a converging lens.

body: Converging lenses fix long sight by shortening the focus. Diverging lenses fix short sight by lengthening the focus.

body: An element or compound with a crystal–like structure. They are the 'building blocks' of rocks.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: crystalline
body: Crystalline describes a rock composed of interlocking crystals. It is ‘crystal–like’.

title: rock

title: Pupils generally confuse the distinctions between a rock and a mineral.
body: Stress and reinforce the definitions of each. Use examples of each and practice classifying them as a mineral or rock.

body: Sedimentary rocks contain distinct grains that are stuck together.

body: Igneous rocks contain crystals that point in many directions; metamorphic rocks contain crystals that mostly line up.

body: Rocks that contain interlocking grains or interlocking crystals are non-porous; rocks that don't are porous.

body: The properties of rock influence their uses.

body: Earth is a spherical, rocky planet with a thin crust, partially covered in water.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Under Earth’s crust is a dense rocky layer, called the mantle.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In the centre of Earth is a solid metallic core surrounded by a liquid outer core.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Temperature and pressure increases towards the centre of Earth, making the inner core extremely hot and solid.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Scientists use models to better understand phenomena, including Earth's structure.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: crust
body: The rocky, outermost layer of Earth.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: mantle
body: A layer of dense rock found below the crust. Parts of it behave as a fluid over very long, geological time scales.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: outer core
body: The outer core is a liquid layer of mostly iron and nickel that lies between the mantle and inner core.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: inner core
body: The inner core is a solid ball of mostly iron that lies at the centre of Earth, within the outer core.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: model
body: Scientists use models as simpler representations of complex things and ideas.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils struggle to appreciate the relative scales between each layer and features of the mantle.
body: Use common models (boiled egg or an orange) to stress the relative sizes and use multiple demonstrations to model features of the mantle.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Occurrences of earthquakes and volcanic eruptions suggest Earth’s layers are not static but interact with each other.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Evidence, such as rock formations and fossils, supports the idea that the continents were once all joined up.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Earth’s crust is broken into pieces known as tectonic plates, which move very, very slowly.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Plate tectonics is a scientific theory that explains how tectonic plates move and interact with each other.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: Plate tectonics help scientists better understand and predict changes to Earth’s surface.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: continental drift
body: A theory that proposed Earth's continents were once one landmass and gradually drifted apart over time.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: continental crust

attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: oceanic crust

attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tectonic plate
body: a large, rigid slab of Earth's lithosphere (outer layer) that sits on the semi-solid asthenosphere beneath it
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: plate tectonics
body: A theory that explains why continental landmasses move due to tectonic plates.
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Some pupils (and teachers and even textbooks) suggest that plate movement is due solely to convection currents.
body: Stress that the understanding of what drives of tectonic plate moment is still developing; using demonstrations to reinforce the current understanding of slab pull and ridge push are helpful. Avoid any demos that reinforce ideas the mantle is liquid.

title: lava

body: a process that forms solid crystals from a saturated solution by evaporating the solvent
attribution_text: A science lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

body: In a crystal, the atoms are all arranged in a very regular pattern.

attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils may sometimes feel that it is cheating to use genre specific conventions, imagining that every idea must be wholely original.
body: All composers will consider elements of genre specific conventions when composing, even if it is to work against them. Using musical ideas that are familiar to a genre can help establish style and provide a good creative starting point.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: genre
body: A style or category of literature.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: instrumentation
body: the combination of musical instruments used in a piece of music
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: structure
body: A structure is the way something is organised.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: stylistic convention
body: a common musical feature that is typical of a particular genre or period
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Pupils can struggle with the balance of repetition and variation, sometimes using either too much or too little repetition.
body: When looking at example compositions emphasize the importance of repetition to establish a memorable idea, and of variation to keep the music interesting. There are different conventions for this balance within different musical genres.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: development
body: the progress of a country in terms of wealth, use of technology and human welfare
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: motif
body: an action or series of actions that are repeated
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: repetition
body: part of a program where one or more commands are run multiple times in a loop
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: variation
body: changing the type of training to keep it interesting and effective
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Some pupils may find it hard mapping out a full structure to a piece early on in the process of composing, preferring instead to fully develop one section before moving on.
body: Although there is no one correct way to compose, it can be useful to map out the structure of a composition early on as it helps to give direction to the composing process and to highlight opportinuties for repetition and contrast.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: contrast
body: a comparison made to show the differences between two or more things, people, or ideas
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Phrase
body: A group of words with no verb
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: section
body: a larger part of a piece (e.g. verse, chorus, A, B)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: structure
body: A structure is the way something is organised.

title: Pupils may think that developing a composition means adding more material or making it more complex.
body: Refining doesn’t always mean adding more. Small, deliberate changes can have a strong impact, and simplicity can often be an effective compositional choice.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Accompaniment
body: An accompaniment is a part in the music that supports the melody.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: articulation
body: the way that a note is played (e.g. staccato, accented, legato)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: refining
body: improving and perfecting a sequence to enhance its quality, precision and overall performance
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: texture
body: the feel or appearance of surfaces, such as rough bark or smooth stones
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: timbre
body: the specific quality of a sound (e.g. shrill, mellow); this is often used to refer to instrument choice as well

body: A simple, well-shaped idea is often more effective than a busy one. Focus on contour and rhythm rather than quantity of notes.

title: Contrast means the sections don't need to relate to each other.
body: Contrasting sections should still share something (an instrument, a rhythm, a key) to feel part of the same piece.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Adding more markings is the same as adding expression.
body: Markings must be appropriate and consistent. A forte marking on a relaxing piece, or dynamics only at the start, do not demonstrate expressive understanding.

title: Annotation means describing what is happening, not explaining why.
body: Simply writing "I used piano here" is not enough. Annotations must explain the reason for a decision and link it clearly to the brief.

title: It is important to use lots of different rhythmic devices.
body: It is more important to use a few rhythmic devices that are effective and idiomatic for the style, rather than using lots of different rhythmic devices.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: cross rhythm
body: a polyrhythm in which two or more of the rhythms 'conflict' and feel like they have a different pulse
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Diminution
body: the process of shortening all of the notes in a melody by the same proportion
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: hemiola
body: when three notes are played over the duration of two or vice versa, creating the feeling of tempo change
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Polyrhythm
body: When multiple rhythms are played at the same time we call this a polyrhythm.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: syncopation
body: rhythms that emphasise the offbeat
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: In a piano trio, the piano plays the accompanying chords, the cello plays the bass line and violin plays the melody.
body: The three instruments serve varied roles in a piano trio. Many composers share the melody and the accompaniment between all three, and have them interact in different ways. It is a versatile ensemble, with lots of potential for interesting textures.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: antiphony
body: where two or more instruments or groups have dialogue (similar to call and response)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Doubling
body: Doubling is the act of becoming twice as many.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: harmonisation
body: where a second part plays the main melody with different notes, creating harmony
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: imitation
body: when a short part of a melody is copied (or 'imitated') in another part
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: polyphony
body: a texture involving more than one equally important melodic line
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: An inverted pedal must be the highest note that is playing.
body: An inverted pedal can be any non-bass note that stays constant while the chords change. This does not have to be the highest part, it can be a middle-pitched part instead.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: countermelody
body: a countermelody is a second melody that plays at the same time as the main melody
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Diminution
body: the process of shortening all of the notes in a melody by the same proportion
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: inverted pedal
body: where a note in a non-bass part stays the same while the chords change around or below it
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: pedal
body: a continuous pitch or note in the music which remains the same as the other harmonies change
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: sequence
body: a series of actions linked together
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: When composing for multiple parts, they should use the same or similar articulation.
body: In certain styles it can be very effective to use contrasting articulation in different parts. This might mean having a legato melody in one part and an accented staccato accompaniment, or any other combination.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: accent
body: symbol added on top of vowels to indicate something about their pronunciation
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: flutter tonguing
body: a brass and woodwind technique that creates a fluttery 'rrr' effect during a note; it is indicated in a score by the tremolo symbol and 'fl.'
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: register
body: level of formality or style of language used, depending on the audience, purpose, and context
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: subito
body: an Italian term indicating that something should happen ‘suddenly’
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: tenuto
body: a type of accent in which a note is given more 'weight' and its full duration
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: A single melody line cannot be prominent in a thick texture.
body: If the rhythms and pitches of the accompaniment 'get in the way' of the melody, it will be inaudible. However, with careful consideration of those elements, the accompaniment can be thick and loud while the melody stays prominent.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: theme and variations
body: a structure based on one main theme that is developed through different variations
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: unison
body: performing the same action, at the same time
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: Every instrument has a defined range.
body: Some instruments (e.g. piano) have a defined range, but not all. Woodwind and brass instruments, for example, have a typical 'normal' range, but advanced players can often play very high notes beyond the top of that range.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: disjunct
body: movement between notes that involves intervals larger than two semitones (moving by leap)
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: range
body: the range of pitches that an instrument is capable of playing
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: register
body: level of formality or style of language used, depending on the audience, purpose, and context
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: A composition should use every possible idiomatic feature from the style.
body: It is normal not to use every single idiomatic feature. Most compositions use a range of idiomatic features with different elements, to help them fit the style effectively. Choose a range of idiomatic features that work well in your composition.
attribution_text: A music lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: The right to freedom of religion or belief is an absolute right.

title: Our changing bodies must match up to the bodies we see in the media to be considered ‘normal’.
body: There is a wide range of ‘normal’ changes that take place during puberty. If a person is worried about anything relating to their body at this time, they can talk to a doctor or trusted adult.
attribution_text: A rshe and pshe lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: acne
body: when your skin gets spots or pimples because of blocked pores, often during puberty
attribution_text: A rshe and pshe lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: body odour
body: a smell that is caused by bacteria on the skin breaking down proteins in sweat; it can become more noticeable in puberty as sweat glands become more active
attribution_text: A rshe and pshe lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: puberty
body: Puberty is a time when human bodies go through changes to become adults that are able to reproduce.
attribution_text: A rshe and pshe lesson by Oak National Academy licensed under Open Government Licence (OGL)

title: All women's health conditions are menstrual disorders.
body: Women's health conditions affect different body systems. Some mainly affect the menstrual cycle, while others affect hormones or several body systems. PMOS is an endocrine condition, although menstrual changes can be one of its symptoms.
